Jonah stopped beneath the unlit arch and waited for Mara to decide what his silence meant.

She reached him in three long steps. The hand he had offered was still out, palm upward. Her fingertips brushed the calluses, the scars, the long fingers.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

“That you believed me?”

She felt his thumb press the center of her palm. “No.”

“Then what?”

Mara lifted her head, making room for a kiss. He kissed her hard, the way people did when they were not ready to say they had been wrong. Her back hit the brickwork of the archway, the cold stone breaking into her spine. He pressed her hair into her shoulders, his body braced in a way that should have made her want to push him away. Instead she slid one hand up his shoulder and let herself feel how much harder he was breathing than she was.

When she moved the hand back down to his chest, he caught it. His grip was tight, but he did not pull her into the touch. She could still take it away.

Mara looked up at the arc of the night sky, the brickwork lit by the light pollution of the city, the faint sound of traffic.

“What are you doing?” Jonah asked.

“Nothing,” she said, and meant it.

He pressed his hand flat against the brick. “Do you think I can’t tell what you’re thinking?”

“I’m thinking about what happens if I do this again. Or if I don’t.”

He stepped away from the wall. The hard pressure of his body against hers vanished, and her hand dropped from his chest.

“Is that why you didn’t call the police?”

Mara felt her pulse jump. She could feel the blood thrumming in her fingertips.

“You could have called them,” Jonah said.

She felt the heat rise in her face and took a deep breath, trying to ground herself in the present.

“I didn’t,” Mara said.

“And why is that?”

Mara looked up at the sky, still trying to steady her breathing.

“It’s not just about me,” she said.

“It never is,” Jonah said. “But it should be.”

Mara felt her pulse jump again, and this time she knew why.

“I didn’t want to make things worse,” she said.

Jonah’s hand was still on her wrist, and she felt the muscles in his arm tighten.

“By reporting a crime?”

Mara let out a long, slow breath.

“No,” she said. “By escalating the situation.”

Jonah’s gaze was still sharp, but his expression had softened slightly.

“What situation?” he asked.

“This situation,” Mara said. “The one where we’re both here, right now, and you’re asking me why I didn’t do something I could have done.”

Jonah’s hand dropped from her wrist, and for a moment there was only silence.

Mara took a step back, and then another.

“I need to go,” she said.

Jonah didn’t move.

Mara walked toward the gate, her steps slow and deliberate.

Jonah watched her go.

Jonah stopped beneath the unlit arch and waited for Mara to decide what his silence meant.

The arc of stone separated them from Fulcrum by two full blocks, but a chill lingered as if he had taken some of the laboratory’s machinery into his hand. Mara pulled the scarf up over her mouth, leaving just enough room for breathing. Her hair was already damp against the back of her neck, and the fog had thickened since they had left the pavilion.

“It’s not cold in Fulcrum,” she said.

“The labs stay calibrated for the machines.”

He put his hand on the wall beside the arch. She did not touch him. She was aware of his presence as if each had a boundary no wider than one step.

“So you keep the air dry,” Mara said. “That’s a choice.”

“It’s a compromise.”

She heard it in his voice and in the space behind his silence. “Someone has to breathe there.”

“Most people,” Jonah admitted. “One is less efficient.”

She pulled the scarf down to keep talking. The air smelled of salt and fog without being either.

“What did you want from me?” Mara asked.

Jonah did not answer immediately. His hand remained on the wall, the weight of it a promise he could not keep.

“I wanted to see how you reacted,” he said. “There are things you do when you think nobody is watching that other people can’t un-see.”

“And?” Mara asked. “Did I do it well?”

“Not badly. But not as well as I might have.”

“You’re telling me a failure is acceptable.”

“I’m telling you that you could still be better.”

It was a cruel thing to say. Jonah knew it was cruel before he finished.

“Because that’s how Fulcrum works,” Mara said.

She stepped back, the bare minimum of movement to separate herself from him. His hand slid down the wall.

“Do I get to see your calibration too?” she asked.

“You don’t need to.”

“Then why do you need mine?”

“Because you’re different.”

“Am I?”

She looked at him in a way that made him uncertain of his own certainty.

Jonah let his hand drop completely. He had nothing to hold against the weight of that silence.

“Because you’re an outsider,” he said. “Because you’re not one of us.”

Mara lifted the scarf again. She spoke through it, the words muffled but precise.

“Am I?” she asked. “Or did you just decide I am?”

“I didn’t decide anything.”

“Then who did? Or is it simply a property of Fulcrum that some people are on the inside and some are on the outside?”

His mouth stayed open because he couldn’t bring himself to lie about how true that was.

“That’s not fair,” Jonah said.

“Fair is not the problem, Jonah. The problem is that you want what you can’t have because you refuse to ask for it.”

She moved close enough to touch him. She didn’t reach out.

“You want me to come back,” Mara said. “You want me to be useful. You want me to be predictable. You don’t want me to be what I actually am.”

“And what are you?” Jonah asked.

The question cost him something he wasn’t sure he wanted to give.

“I’m a person,” Mara said. “I have a name. I have a face. I have a life outside your damn institution.”

“And?”

“And you have a choice about whether to let me into yours.”

He wanted to tell her it wasn’t that simple. He didn’t want to admit that she was right.

“Do you want that choice?” he asked. “Really?”

Her scarf dropped away from her lips.

“Yes,” she said.

It was a small word. But the way she said it changed everything between them.

“Then make it,” Mara told him. “Choose.”

His hand found hers without meaning to. She didn’t pull away.

“What if I’m not ready?” Jonah asked.

“Then tell me what you need,” she said. “But stop pretending like I’m not real. Stop pretending like I’m not here.”

He couldn’t look away from her. The fog had taken the last light with it, but there was enough from the streetlamps to see the small motion of her breath, the way her eyes stayed fixed on his face as if he were the last truth left in the world.

“You’re not,” Mara said softly. “And I don’t think you ever were.”

“Then what was I?”

“You were afraid.”

“Of what?”

“Of losing control.”

“And?”

“And you still are.”

It was a blow, but one delivered without malice.

“I’m sorry,” Jonah said.

Mara touched his wrist. He almost didn’t feel it because the rest of him felt like the weight of every choice he had made and every one he hadn’t.

“You don’t have to be,” she said. “But you do have to stop pretending like I’m not here.”

“I’m not.”

“Then look at me.”

He did.

She was still there. Solid. Real. Unavoidable.

“You’re not going to make this easy for me, are you?”

“I’m not going to make it hard. But I’m not going to pretend like it’s something it’s not.”

“And what is it?”

“It’s real.”

His hand tightened on hers.

“Then I’m here,” Mara said. “And you’re here. And we both have choices.”

He nodded.

She leaned in just a little. His breath caught.

“Tell me what you want,” Mara said.

Her voice was low but clear. He wasn’t sure he had ever heard such a simple demand.

“I want—” he began.

She brought her free hand to his face.

The touch was light but firm. She looked at him like he was the only thing in the world.

“Don’t lie,” Mara said. “Not here. Not now. Not to me.”

“I won’t,” Jonah said.

His hand moved of its own will, his fingers curling against her neck. He felt her pulse beneath his skin.

Mara tilted her head. Her eyes never left his.

“Then tell me.”

“I want—”

He stopped.

“You’re stalling,” she said.

“I’m not.”

“Then tell me.”

Jonah let the breath out.

“I want—” he said.

She leaned in just a little farther.

“Finish it,” Mara whispered.

His lips brushed hers.

She didn’t pull away.

He stopped.

She didn’t push him.

“You still have a choice,” Mara said.

Her mouth was so close he could feel the heat of it.

“You can say no.”

Her breath was warm on his skin.

“You can ask me to wait.”

His pulse raced in his wrist.

“You can ask me to leave.”

Her eyes remained fixed on his face.

“But if you want to kiss me—”

She leaned in just a little farther.

His hand tightened on hers.

“Then kiss me.”

His lips touched hers.

Mara didn’t move.

Jonah closed his eyes.

Her mouth tasted like cardamom and honey.

He opened his eyes again.

Mara was still looking at him.

“You can still stop,” she said softly.

Her voice was like a thread pulled taut between them.

Jonah didn’t move.

Mara leaned in just a little farther.

Her mouth met his again.

She didn’t kiss back.

He didn’t pull away.

Mara opened her eyes.

Jonah looked at her.

She let the breath out.

“You’re not going to make this easy for me, are you?”

His mouth was still pressed to hers.

Mara tilted her head just a little.

She pulled away.

Jonah didn’t follow.

“You still have a choice,” Mara said softly.

She looked at him in a way that made him want to tell her the truth.

Jonah let go of her hand.

“I made my choice,” he said.

Mara took a step back.

He watched her.

“I’m glad,” she said.

Jonah didn’t move.

Mara put her hand on the wall beside the arch.

She turned to leave.

Jonah watched her walk away.

The fog closed behind her.

He stood there for a long time.

END

Simon set the recovered drive on the bedroom table and waited for Esther to ask why its seal was broken.

She put her laptop on top of him instead.

He moved slightly to avoid his own drive, his own data, and his own risk. “Where did you want the backup?”

“Right there. It’s a physical separation, isn’t it?”

“And you call me paranoid.”

“I call it a feature. It’s why you survived.”

Her screen came on. The drive spun. He closed his eyes for the brief grace before the light would demand his attention.

“You are the reason,” Esther said. “That was your drive. You built this. You were there.”

It had been his drive, his data, his risk. The thing that had cost her the rescue.

Simon pressed his cheek against her waist. “You survived too.”

Her body did not stiffen, but something did. He turned his head. Esther sat hunched above the screen. His shadow crossed her cheekbones.

“No thanks to me.”

“We don’t know that.”

“I know it.”

“Then you don’t know what I know.”

“I know you were there.”

He touched her wrist. “You know what I told you.”

Her hand stayed on the keyboard. She did not move away or give him back the drive. She did not kiss him either.

It took twenty minutes. The drive finished copying to the laptop. Simon got out of bed, went into the bathroom, and brushed his teeth. He was washing his face when Esther came in.

The towel was over his shoulder. He turned and waited.

The bathroom was too narrow for both of them. Esther stood in the doorway. She had changed into a T-shirt with his logo on it, white on gray.

The drive had been in his pocket all day. When he went to work, she knew what it was. When he returned without her, she knew it had come back with him. She had waited until the room was dark before touching him.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

“I’m not.”

“Then—”

She turned and walked past him. He watched her until the bedroom light came on. The drive lay on the bed.

Simon moved first.

The thing he had recovered was on the table. The thing he had lost was in the bed.

“You didn’t tell me about the seal,” he said.

Esther touched the case.

“It wasn’t broken.”

He moved nearer.

She turned the case over. The seam was straight. “The seal was good. They didn’t access the data.”

“But they opened it.”

“Yes.”

Her voice remained flat. Esther knew when someone else was right, and she was not good at giving away ground.

“And you didn’t tell me about that either.”

“It was minor.”

“You used the minor word.”

He took her wrist in his hand. The skin felt too delicate for him to hold.

“The minor word,” she said. “You were the one who taught me minor words.”

It had been a joke the first time. It had become a warning. When Esther was sorry, she apologized. When she used the minor word, the danger was real.

“If I had known about the broken seal, I would have come,” she said. “I would have risked you.”

He sat beside her on the bed, close enough that he could feel the heat in her chest. The laptop sat closed beside them.

“And you thought that was my preference,” he said. “That the possibility of bringing data back was more important to me than the person I would bring back with it.”

She pressed her forehead to his shoulder.

His T-shirt smelled like soap. The white logo on gray did not look wrong in the dim light.

“I didn’t think you didn’t care. I thought you knew more. I thought I knew what mattered to you, and it wasn’t enough. I don’t know why I thought that.”

“You thought I was replaceable,” he said. “You thought there was more to rescue than me.”

Her head stayed against his shoulder. Her fingers drew slow circles on his chest.

“I thought you were better at risk than I am.”

The admission made him shiver. He knew where her fears were sharp. They came from the same place as his.

“That’s not a skill,” he said. “It’s a mistake.”

“I know.”

“And I’m not better than you.”

“No. You’re smarter.”

“I’m not smarter than you.”

“But you are.”

Simon bent over her hand where it rested on the bed, holding it between both of his.

“Then I’m not good at it,” he said. “I’m not good at being smarter than you.”

She pressed her forehead to his chest and breathed his words into the cotton.

“I missed you,” she said.

“I missed you too.”

“More than I missed anything.”

Simon put his hand on the back of her neck. She still smelled like soap. Her hair was short, damp at the ends.

He kissed her. She kissed him back.

“I thought I could still stop him. I didn’t think about you.”

“I had to know it wasn’t there first.”

Esther’s lips pressed together. Then she leaned back against the wall and smiled. “It wasn’t.”

“No.”

“You’ve been quiet for a week.”

He pressed both hands against the door. “It would have been a mistake to tell you how quiet.”

She slid a finger inside her shirt collar. Her pulse moved slowly and exactly under her skin. Simon tracked it to her throat and thought for one second it had stopped. Then he realized how long the room had been quiet.

Esther looked away. “Don’t do that.”

“Why?”

“You know why.”

“I’m not trying to make you do anything.”

“You don’t know what I think.”

“Then tell me what you’re thinking.”

He heard his voice in the room and felt a small private regret.

Esther stepped closer. Her chest brushed his shoulder.

“No,” she said. “Because if I tell you, it’ll stop being real.”

Simon looked at her. “That’s not a real thought.”

“Oh, it is.”

“What else did you think about while you were waiting for me to die?”

“I didn’t. I was in shock. I thought I would die.”

“Yes.”

“You said I wouldn’t make it. You said I should stop.”

“And you ignored me.”

“Because you’d done something else you didn’t tell me.”

Esther took a step back. “I needed to know whether we could still win this.”

“By yourself?”

“I knew I wouldn’t have to.”

She gave him one clear, certain look. Her finger moved back down to the necklace clasp at her throat. Her pulse quickened there.

“I kept you alive,” Esther said.

Simon looked at his hands. His left ring finger felt like someone else’s.

“I’ll kill him,” he said. “For that.”

Esther’s breath caught.

“Oh no,” she said. “I want you to kill him too.”

text:
The tea was exactly the temperature Mara would have chosen for herself, which made refusing it feel theatrical.

She had not been expecting that.

She closed her notebook, pushed it across the table, and turned back toward the quietest corner of the circle. A new pair was working through the calibration prompt. Their breathing had not yet changed, which meant they were not there yet.

Mara rested her elbows on the table. She had not slept in forty-eight hours. Adrian would send her to bed. He had to; he was the responsible adult in the room. If she let Livia convince her to stay for a second alignment session, her choices would not be her own the next time she made one.

“Your left temple,” Livia said.

Mara raised both hands to cover it.

“No, don’t,” Livia said.

She placed one cool hand against Mara’s shoulder. Her hair fell across Mara’s chest, and Mara could see the pale whorls of her breath in the circle’s ambient light.

“You’re trying to get to the other side of tired,” Livia said. “There’s nothing there but less control.”

Mara could not be convinced to argue. She opened her fingers and let them lie on the table.

Livia settled beside her, close enough that Mara had to adjust her left elbow to avoid crowding Livia’s right foot.

“Have you ever tried a second alignment?”

“This is a first-alignment institute.”

Livia touched Mara’s hair, then withdrew her hand as though remembering who owned it.

“No one would know.”

“You would.”

Livia put her left hand flat against Mara’s back. “I’m good at secrets.”

The weight of Livia’s palm was warm and perfectly still. Mara wanted it.

“You’re a terrible secret-keeper,” Mara said.

“True. But you need a little of that right now.”

Mara pressed both palms to the table. “What I need is a ten-hour sleep debt.”

“What you need,” Livia said, “is to be cared for in a way that keeps you where you are. And I am an excellent caregiver.”

That was a claim that required controls, but Mara had already exhausted her ability to invent one.

“I’ll take your word for it,” she said. “For now.”

Livia settled her left elbow on the table, wrist across the back of Mara’s hand. The pressure was gentle enough to be taken away if Mara moved.

“This is a consent-based activity,” Livia said. “You can say no to all of it or to a part of it.”

Mara let her palm lie under Livia’s fingers. “How would you do it if I were unconscious?”

“I wouldn’t.”

Mara looked up.

“I don’t help unconscious people,” Livia said. “They’re too good at resisting.”

Mara considered taking her hand back.

Livia did not change the pressure of her palm.

“I can’t tell which side you’re on,” Mara said.

Livia gave a small smile. “That’s the point.”

The calibration pair across the circle began to speak, softly. Mara turned her head toward them.

Livia’s fingers tightened against the back of her hand, just enough to make her wrist shift.

Mara turned back. The pressure stayed.

“There is one small condition,” Livia said.

“I am listening.”

“If I manage to keep you aligned for another ninety minutes, you will agree not to sleep before eight A.M. tomorrow.”

“Eight A.M. tomorrow?”

“Midnight is the only other time I’ll be here for alignment. You can choose.”

Mara pressed both palms against the table. “Why are you doing this?”

Livia took her hand and pulled it onto Mara’s lap. The contact stayed gentle but became impossible to ignore.

“I believe in care that is also a risk,” Livia said. “And in risks that become rewards for people who know how to take them. You are clearly both.”

Mara’s left hand remained in Livia’s. Her right hand rested on the table, half an inch from the sensor puck’s soft blue light.

Livia shifted closer.

“You are welcome,” Livia said, “to ask me to stop. To name my touches and tell me not to repeat them. To remind me who owns what choices.”

Mara did not respond.

Livia leaned forward, close enough that her hair fell across Mara’s wrist. “And I am going to give you enough care that the first time you remember your own boundaries will be after we are finished.”

That was the most honest thing she’d said all night. It made Mara want to press Livia against the table and tell her not to ruin Mara’s control by knowing exactly what it would feel like.

Livia’s thumb came up to the tender skin just below Mara’s wrist. She traced one slow line from pulse to crease, her nail grazing the inside of Mara’s arm where it was soft and exposed.

The line traveled toward Mara’s pulse point, where it would have settled if it could. Livia stopped just short of it.

Mara breathed out.

Livia pressed against Mara’s wrist again, light enough to be lifted with one small movement. Her other hand stayed against Mara’s back, anchoring them both in the space between “too little” and “too much.”

“I’ve spent thirty years being a good girl,” Livia said. “I’m very interested in being a bad one.”

The words were spoken close enough to be a risk. Livia was aware of this. She was not avoiding it.

The pulse point at Mara’s wrist beat with deliberate speed, reminding them both what a touch there would mean.

Livia let go.

“You’re not interested in being my bad girl,” Mara said.

Livia smiled, pleased but not defensive.

“I’m not,” she said.

Mara wanted the touch to come back. She wanted the touch to stay away. She wanted the pulse to steady under Livia’s fingers and for Livia to know exactly when it would.

Livia let Mara keep her hand, untouched but not unclaimed.

“You are interested in a kind of badness that’s still good,” Livia said. “You’re looking for the line where control turns into something you can let yourself care about.”

She touched the back of Mara’s hand. Her nail traced one small arc there before lifting away.

The line beneath her thumb stayed open.

Livia watched Mara for any sign of retreat.

Mara stayed in the space Livia had given her.

Livia did not take it back. She did not rush toward the risk. She settled Mara’s hand on her lap, shifted one bare foot to press against Mara’s shin, and gave her one small exhale, as though offering proof that there was still room to breathe.

Mara closed her eyes.

Livia did not ask what it would feel like to have her touch stay there.

She waited for Mara to look at her.

When she did, Livia leaned back in the circle, just far enough to give Mara the choice of stepping toward it.

Mara did not move.

Livia watched her. She did not remove her foot or hand, but she did not give any sign that she needed Mara’s response.

The calibration pair across the circle had gone silent. No one had moved.

Livia’s foot rested against Mara’s shin, warm but not pressing. Her hand remained on Mara’s wrist, holding without claiming it.

She did not ask Mara to move closer.

Mara moved closer.

Livia stayed.

Her hair fell across Mara’s wrist. Her breath was close enough to feel. Her hand lay open on the back of Mara’s hand.

Mara let her palm rest there, not claiming the touch but not taking it back either.

Livia waited.

There was enough risk in this to make it worth having.

There was not enough control to keep Mara from wanting more.

Livia did not fill the space.

She left room for Mara to step into it.

Mara did not move.

Livia smiled and gave her one more small exhale, as though offering proof that there was still room to breathe.

Mara looked up.

Livia did not respond.

She did not ask Mara to speak.

She did not fill the silence.

Mara closed her eyes.

She opened them to find Livia watching her.

“I need ten hours of sleep,” Mara said.

Livia’s smile stayed, but her gaze softened.

“I’m not asking you to stay awake,” Livia said. “I’m asking you to let me stay with you while you sleep.”

The words hung in the room, light enough to be taken away with one small movement.

Mara wanted the touch to come back. She wanted the touch to stay away.

Livia did not take either choice from her.

She simply sat with her foot against Mara’s shin and her hand resting on the back of her hand.

“You are welcome,” Livia said, “to ask me to stop.”

Mara did not move.

Livia waited.

The risk was enough to make it worth having.

The control was enough
